meta.title: Who really said "You Are Only Interested in Art and I Am Only Interested in Money"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Earliest print: Baltimore American, 1 May 1921. Shaw retold it in 1922 and 1926 in different words; a 1937 book credits the wording to a publicist.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'You Are Only Interested in Art and I Am Only Interested in Money'?
meta.ogDescription: Shaw's jab at Samuel Goldwyn reached print in a May 1921 London cable, but Shaw retold it twice in other words and a publicist claimed the famous version.

answer.label: Attributed to
answer.sourceLine: Shaw’s parting shot to film producer Samuel Goldwyn reached print in a London cable published by the Baltimore American on 1 May 1921, and Shaw claimed the exchange as his own when he retold it in 1922 and again in 1926 — but with different wording each time. A 1937 biography of Goldwyn credits the polished version everyone quotes to the producer’s publicity chief, and Quote Investigator concludes only that Shaw “likely did make the statement” ↗. No text in Shaw’s own hand carries this sentence.

source.excerpt: Mr. Goldwyn is a ready talker and G.B.S. being Irish, was a little behind him at times. After going over the entire film situation in a discussion lasting several hours, Mr. Shaw closed the interview as follows: “Well, Mr. Goldwyn, there is not much use in going on. There is this difference between you and me: You are only interested in art and I am only interested in money.”
source.trailTitle: How the line got into print
trail: 1 May 1921 — a special cable from London, printed in the Baltimore American under the headline “Shaw Refuses to Write for Movies,” carries the earliest known printing: Shaw closes the interview with the art-and-money line ↗. Reprints follow in Springfield, Illinois and Columbia, South Carolina later that month.

21 May 1921 — New York’s Evening Telegram runs the story from its own copy rather than as a reprint, framing it differently but ending on the same sentence: “Do you know, Mr. Goldwyn, there is a radical difference between you and me?” ↗

1922 and 1926 — Shaw tells the story on himself twice more, once to the Incorporated Society of Authors, Playwrights and Composers and once to an International News Service reporter, using a different phrasing on each occasion ↗.

1937 — Alva Johnston’s The Great Goldwyn (Random House) claims Goldwyn’s publicity chief Howard Dietz compressed Shaw’s words into the famous form and had it released in London; the passage is quoted in full by Quote Investigator ↗, which nonetheless comes down on Shaw’s side.
source.excerptNote: As transcribed by Quote Investigator from the Baltimore American of 1 May 1921, the earliest printing it was able to locate. Note that the version which circulates today — “The trouble, Mr. Goldwyn, is that you are only interested in art and I am only interested in money” — is a later, tighter form, and it is the one a 1937 Goldwyn biography attributes to a publicist rather than to Shaw.

source.rightsNote: The wording survives because American newspapers printed it: the Baltimore American of 1 May 1921, its reprints later that month, and the further reports of Shaw’s own retellings in 1922 and 1926. All of those are United States publications from well before the 1931 public-domain cutoff, so the printed text is free to reproduce. That is a statement about the newspaper text only — it is not a warrant that Shaw framed the sentence in exactly these words.

author.name: George Bernard Shaw
author.kicker: The man who read the contract
author.heading: Who was George Bernard Shaw?
author.metaLine: 1856–1950 · Irish playwright, critic and Nobel laureate
author.bio: Shaw was an Irish playwright, critic and polemicist who won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1925 and later became the first person to hold both a Nobel and an Academy Award, the latter for the screenplay of Pygmalion. He was also a famously hard-headed man of business: he refused the money that came with the Nobel on the grounds that his readers and audiences already provided him with more than enough, and he told a room of fellow authors that at the start of his career he had never signed an agreement he had not drafted himself. That combination — the moralist who reads the contract — is exactly what makes the Goldwyn story sound like him.

copyAttribution: "You are only interested in art and I am only interested in money." — attributed to George Bernard Shaw, addressing film producer Samuel Goldwyn. Earliest documented printing: the Baltimore American, 1 May 1921, from a London cable. Shaw retold the exchange himself in 1922 and 1926, using different wording each time, and a 1937 biography of Goldwyn credits this polished version to publicist Howard Dietz. quotle.info

misattribution.heading: Right name, contested sentence
misattribution.intro: Nobody seriously doubts that Shaw and Goldwyn met, or that Shaw walked away having made a joke at the producer’s expense. What is contested is the sentence. Three different wordings survive from the 1920s alone, and the one everybody quotes is the one a Hollywood press agent later claimed as his own handiwork.

items.why: Alva Johnston’s 1937 biography The Great Goldwyn says a version of the conversation was cabled to Dietz, who “compressed Shaw’s words” into “The trouble, Mr. Goldwyn, is that you are only interested in art and I am only interested in money” — then had it cabled back to London and released there. Norman Zierold’s The Moguls (1969) repeats the account and notes that this is the form which gained the widest circulation ↗.

The Baltimore American of 1 May 1921 has Shaw “closing the interview” after several hours of discussion; New York’s Evening Telegram of 21 May 1921, working from its own copy rather than a reprint, has him delivering “an unexpected retort” and opening with “Do you know, Mr. Goldwyn, there is a radical difference between you and me?” Both end on the same sentence ↗, but neither is a stenographic record.

In 1922 Shaw told a society of authors: “The difficulty between us is that you care for nothing but art and I seem to care for nothing but money.” By 1926 it had become “you’re an artist and care only about art, while I’m only a tradesman and care only about money.” Quote Investigator judges the 1926 telling the most eloquently humorous of the three ↗ — and it is not the one anyone repeats.

misattribution.truthLine: Shaw really did say something very like this to Samuel Goldwyn, and he cheerfully took credit for it twice. But the crisp sentence in circulation is the press’s version of his joke, not a line documented in Shaw’s own writing — Quote Investigator’s verdict is that Shaw “likely” made the 1921 statement, with Howard Dietz conceivably contributing ↗.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Goldwyn called on Shaw in England to sign him for the movies. In 1921 the film business was buying literary prestige wherever it could, and Shaw was the prize that kept saying no — he turned film companies down right through the silent era, “even as the proffered sums grew higher and higher” ↗.

The joke works because it inverts the roles everyone expects: the Hollywood money man pleading for art, the playwright demanding cash. Shaw was not confessing to greed. He was warning that a producer who opens by talking about elevating the public is a producer who has not yet talked about terms. He said so out loud the following year, telling a society of authors that it is “not dishonest to get the best terms” and that the producer could look after the art ↗.
context.detailsSummary: Why the publicist claim is plausible but not decisive
detailsBody: Alva Johnston was writing in 1937 about a conversation from 1921, in a breezy biography stuffed with anecdotes, and he does not say how he knew what Howard Dietz did. Hollywood publicity departments really did manufacture wit for their bosses, which is why the claim lands. But the wording Johnston gives Dietz is not the wording the newspapers cabled from London in May 1921: the press text runs “There is this difference between you and me,” while the Dietz form is “The trouble, Mr. Goldwyn, is that…” A press agent tightening a line that already existed is a smaller claim than a press agent inventing one.

The strongest argument for Shaw is Shaw. He performed the story twice more — in 1922 to a room full of authors, in 1926 to a wire-service reporter — both times casting himself as the tradesman and Goldwyn as the aesthete. A man handed a joke by somebody else’s publicist might have let it quietly stand; Shaw kept telling it. That is the reasoning behind Quote Investigator’s conclusion, and it is why this page reads “attributed” rather than “fabricated.”

sourcesVerified.claim: The earliest located printing is the Baltimore American, 1 May 1921 ('Shaw Refuses to Write for Movies', special cable to the New York Herald and the Baltimore American, dateline London, sec. 2, p. 1, col. 2), reading 'Well, Mr. Goldwyn, there is not much use in going on. There is this difference between you and me: You are only interested in art and I am only interested in money.' The New York Evening Telegram of 21 May 1921 ran an independent version. Shaw retold the exchange in 1922 (Philadelphia Inquirer, 28 May) as 'The difficulty between us is that you care for nothing but art and I seem to care for nothing but money' and in 1926 (Evening Tribune, San Diego, 9 October, INS, by H. K. Reynolds) as 'you're an artist and care only about art, while I'm only a tradesman and care only about money'. Alva Johnston's The Great Goldwyn (1937) says publicist Howard Dietz compressed Shaw's words into 'The trouble, Mr. Goldwyn, is that you are only interested in art and I am only interested in money' and had it cabled back to London; Norman Zierold's The Moguls (1969, p. 128) repeats this and says that form 'gained the widest circulation'. QI concludes Shaw 'likely did make the statement' and that it is 'conceivable that Howard Dietz offered some input'. QI also calls the 1926 telling the most eloquently humorous version. Shaw's 1922 advice to authors included 'It is not dishonest to get the best terms' and 'You look after the art. I'll look after the money.'

The Internet Archive holds a scan of The Great Goldwyn by Alva Johnston, published by Random House, New York, 1937 (verified via the archive.org metadata API: title 'The great Goldwyn', creator 'Johnston, Alva', date 1937, publisher 'New York : Random House, Inc.'). NOTE: the item has no search-inside index (the full-text API returns 'No hOCR or Abbyy file present'), so this link confirms only the book's existence and edition, NOT the Dietz passage on pages 59-60 — that passage is cited to Quote Investigator, which verified it on paper.

George Bernard Shaw was born 26 July 1856 and died 2 November 1950; he was an Irish playwright, critic and polemicist; he won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1925; he was the first person to have been awarded both a Nobel Prize and an Oscar (for the 1938 Pygmalion screenplay); he rejected the monetary component of the Nobel, saying his readers and audiences provide him with more than sufficient money; and he held contempt for Hollywood and its aesthetic values.

Howard Dietz (8 September 1896 – 30 July 1983) served as publicist and director of advertising for Goldwyn Pictures and later MGM, becoming MGM's Vice President in Charge of Publicity in 1942. The page makes no mention of George Bernard Shaw or the 'only interested in art' quotation.

Wikiquote's George Bernard Shaw page does not carry this quotation in any section — not in Sourced, Attributed, Disputed or Misattributed — and contains no mention of Samuel Goldwyn. Verified by fetching the page on 1 September 2026.
